title: Forgive before sleep
hook: the bedtime Shema and forgiving anyone who hurt you
tomorrow: the world stands on three things, says a sage. which fits in a day?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the merchant at the till: count the day fairly, find the leak, close the book. Look back kindly. But some entries won't close, because someone else wrote them.

Bedtime is when the day's arguments come back for a rematch: the thing someone said, the thing you should have said back, the credit somebody else took. The lights are off and the replay is on. The Talmud remembers a sage, Mar Zutra, who had a sentence for exactly that moment. When he went up to bed, he would say: I forgive anyone who has troubled me. That's the sentence. Now, what it does, and what it doesn't.
screen: `LIGHTS OFF, REPLAY ON.` → `MAR ZUTRA GOES UP TO BED.` → `"I FORGIVE ANYONE WHO TROUBLED ME."`

segments.voice: Mar Zutra's line grew into a prayer. In the prayer book, before the Shema said in bed, comes a paragraph: Master of the world, I forgive anyone who angered or wronged me, in body, in money, in honor. Then it goes further: may no one be punished because of me. The bedtime Shema itself leans on a Psalm: "commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still." The Talmud reads that verse as the day ending with the Shema, in bed. So the order is forgive, then hear, then sleep. What does forgiving mean here? The Hebrew word is mechilah, letting go of a claim, the way a lender lets go of a debt. It isn't a verdict that what happened was fine. It doesn't require a phone call, a hug, or pretending. It's a decision about what comes to bed with you. You can still speak up tomorrow; you just don't sleep holding the bill. For serious harm the road is longer, and nobody is asked to pretend; the prayer is there again the next night. Something to tell a friend tonight: the prayer doesn't stop at forgiving. It asks that the other person not be punished on your account.
screen: `MASTER OF THE WORLD, I FORGIVE.` · `FORGIVE, THEN HEAR, THEN SLEEP.` · `MECHILAH: LETTING GO OF A CLAIM.` · `NOT A VERDICT. NOT PRETENDING.` · then, large: `FORGIVE BEFORE SLEEPING.`

segments.voice: Bring one small hurt from today to mind, the smallest one you can find. Say Mar Zutra's sentence quietly, in your own voice: I forgive anyone who troubled me. Then let your shoulders drop and breathe out slowly, like setting a heavy bag down beside the bed.
screen: `ONE SMALL HURT.` · `"I FORGIVE ANYONE WHO TROUBLED ME."` · `SET THE BAG DOWN.`

segments.voice: Forgive before sleep: the paragraph before the bedtime Shema, letting go of the day's claims against others so they don't come to bed with you.
The line for tonight: forgive before sleeping. Tomorrow you can still speak up; tonight you put the bill down.

howItsDone: The bedtime Shema (Kriat Shema al haMitah) is said in bed before sleep; in the prayer book it opens with a paragraph forgiving anyone who caused harm that day. Parents often say the first line of the Shema with young children at bedtime.

notes: Megillah 28a: Mar Zutra's practice paraphrased ('I forgive anyone who has troubled me'); confirm wording and that it describes a habit.
Prayer-book paragraph paraphrased; versions differ slightly (Ashkenazi and Sephardi). Confirm 'in body, in money, in honor' and 'may no one be punished because of me'.
Mechilah as 'letting go of a claim, like a lender lets go of a debt': standard usage (mechilat chov); confirm.
